title: Scarlett Johansson Leads Radical Reboot in ‘The Exorcist: Martyrs’ Trailer – Hollywood Reporter Exclusive
body:
The horror world is buzzing with the first glimpse of a new Exorcist film that promises to reshape the franchise’s mythos. Writer‑director Mike Flanagan, fresh off the critical success of “The Haunting of Hill House” and “The Midnight Club,” has been tapped by Universal to helm “The Exorcist: Martyrs,” a project that pairs his signature psychological dread with a high‑profile cast led by Scarlett Johansson. The teaser trailer, released this week, offers a stark, atmospheric vision that diverges sharply from the 1973 classic while hinting at a fresh narrative direction that could finally revive a series that has stumbled through numerous reboots and sequels over the past three decades.

Flanagan’s involvement marks a significant shift in Universal’s strategy. After the tepid reception of “The Exorcist” (2020) and the abandoned “Exorcist: Believer” plans, the studio appears to be resetting its approach, moving away from straightforward remakes toward a more auteur‑driven interpretation. Known for weaving intricate character studies into supernatural frameworks, Flanagan is expected to deepen the series’ theological questions while retaining the visceral scares that made the original a cultural touchstone. The trailer’s muted palette, slow‑burn pacing, and emphasis on sound design suggest a film that will rely less on jump scares and more on lingering dread—a hallmark of Flanagan’s recent work.

Scarlett Johansson’s casting adds both star power and narrative intrigue. While the actress has not disclosed the specifics of her role, the trailer hints at a mother‑figure grappling with an unseen, malevolent presence that threatens her family. Johansson’s recent pivot toward more nuanced, character‑driven projects aligns with the film’s apparent focus on personal terror over spectacle. Her involvement also signals Universal’s willingness to invest heavily in talent to attract broader audiences beyond traditional horror fans, a tactic that could pay dividends if the film balances critical acclaim with box‑office viability.

The subtitle “Martyrs” further distinguishes this entry from its predecessors. Historically, the term has been associated with the 1978 “Exorcist II: The Heretic,” which introduced a subplot about a group of children with psychic abilities. Flanagan’s teaser, however, appears to reinterpret the concept, possibly exploring themes of sacrifice and faith through a contemporary lens. Early reports suggest the screenplay will delve into the psychological toll of exorcism on both the possessed and the exorcist, echoing the moral ambiguities that Flanagan explored in “Midnight Mass.” If executed effectively, this could revitalize the franchise’s core philosophical conflict—faith versus doubt—while offering fresh visual storytelling.

Industry analysts view the project as a litmus test for Universal’s broader horror slate, which has seen mixed results in recent years. The studio’s “Dark Universe” ambitions have largely faltered, prompting a pivot toward director‑led, story‑first productions. Success with “The Exorcist: Martyrs” could validate this new direction and encourage similar collaborations with visionary filmmakers. Conversely, a misstep might reinforce skepticism about the franchise’s longevity, especially given the saturated market of legacy horror reboots.

As production ramps up for a slated 2027 release, anticipation is already building among fans and critics alike. The trailer’s restrained yet unsettling tone suggests that Flanagan intends to honor the original’s legacy while forging a distinct path forward. If the film delivers on its promise of psychological depth and atmospheric terror, it could not only resurrect a beloved but fractured property but also set a new benchmark for horror storytelling in the studio era. All eyes will be on the final cut, which may finally give the Exorcist a worthy rebirth after years of creative misfires.
